h1: Whisky route to market in India
title: Whisky Route to Market in India | Craft Beer School
desc: How whisky moves from distillery to consumer in India: state models, corporations, listings, permits, channels and what the sales data means.
teaser: There is no single Indian whisky market. There are dozens of state markets, each with its own route from distillery to glass.
standfirst: Getting a bottle of whisky from a distillery to a consumer in India is a different journey in almost every state. For sales, marketing and analytics teams, this guide maps the common routes and explains why the same brand can behave so differently across a state border.
sections: Alcohol is a state business in India

Alcohol for human consumption sits outside GST in India. Each state sets its own excise duty, licences, pricing rules and sales channels. A few states prohibit alcohol altogether, including Gujarat and Bihar. So a national whisky brand is really a collection of state businesses that share a label and a liquid.

For anyone reading a sales dashboard, this is the first thing to understand. A national total is the sum of many separate markets, each with its own calendar, tax changes and buyers. Two states can move in opposite directions in the same month for reasons that have nothing to do with consumers. Our guide to the Indian whisky market gives the wider picture.
The basic chain from distillery to glass

The simplest version of the route looks like this:

  1. The whisky is made or blended and bottled at a licensed plant, under excise supervision.
  2. It is held in a bonded warehouse until duty is paid or the stock is moved under permit.
  3. It passes to a wholesaler, which in some states is a government corporation.
  4. The wholesaler supplies licensed retail shops (the off-trade) and licensed bars, hotels and restaurants (the on-trade).
  5. The consumer buys a bottle in a shop or a drink at a bar.

A separate channel supplies the armed forces through defence canteens, on its own terms. Each step needs licences, permits and records. Rules vary by state and change, so teams work from the current notification for each state.

States organise this chain in different ways. Broadly:

  • Government wholesale, private retail. A state corporation is the only wholesaler. Producers sell to it and licensed private shops and bars buy from it.
  • Government wholesale and retail. The state also runs the shops. Tamil Nadu and Kerala are well known examples.
  • Private wholesale and retail. The state licenses private distributors and shops, sometimes allocating retail licences by auction or lottery.

The model changes how a brand is sold. Where the state runs both wholesale and retail, listings and shelf space depend heavily on the state's buying decisions. Where retail is private, the sales team can work directly with shop owners and bars.

Before a whisky can be sold in a state, its brand and label usually have to be registered with that state's excise department, often for each excise year. The price has to be declared and approved. In states with a government wholesaler, the brand also has to be listed by the corporation before shops can order it.

These steps take time and money for every state, every brand and often every pack size. A new launch planned for ten states is really ten separate approval processes running to ten calendars. Missing a registration window can keep a brand off the shelf for months.
Moving stock between states needs permits

Whisky cannot simply be trucked from one state to another. The sending state issues an export permit and the receiving state an import permit, with transport passes for the journey. Duty is generally collected by the state where the whisky will be sold.

To reduce the cost and delay, many producers bottle in several states, either in their own plants or through licensed bottling partners. The blend or bulk spirit is moved under permit and bottled closer to the market. That is why the bottling address on the same brand can differ from state to state.
Advertising limits make the shelf matter more

Direct advertising of alcohol is heavily restricted in India. That pushes much of the brand effort into the places where the trade is allowed to work: retail shelves, bar menus, trade relationships and events within the rules. Our guide to surrogate advertising rules explains the limits.

So distribution and visibility do more of the work that media would do in other categories. A brand that is listed but poorly placed in a state may sell far below one with a smaller budget and better shelf presence. Sales teams in India often think of availability as their main lever.
What the sales numbers actually measure

Whisky companies usually track at least two sales figures. Primary sales are what the company sells into the first buyer, such as a state corporation or a distributor. Secondary sales are what that buyer sells on to shops and bars. Depletions are what leaves retail to consumers, when that data exists. Our guide to primary and secondary sales explains how they differ.

Primary sales can be pushed or held back for reasons such as duty changes, year-end targets or a corporation's stock policy. Secondary and depletion data are closer to real demand. A practical first step for any analyst: pick your three biggest states, write down the route to market for each one and mark where your sales data is captured. The gaps explain more of the strange months than any model will.
faqs: Is there one route to market for whisky in India?
No. Each state sets its own system. Some use a government wholesaler, some run retail as well and some license private wholesalers and shops.
Why do brands bottle in several states?
Moving finished stock between states needs export and import permits and can add cost and delay. Bottling closer to the market reduces both.
What is the difference between primary and secondary sales?
Primary sales are what the company sells to its first buyer, such as a state corporation. Secondary sales are what that buyer sells on to shops and bars.
